summary: At just 1.9 square miles, West Hollywood packs roughly 18,500 people per square mile — denser than San Francisco — yet sits wedged against the base of the Hollywood Hills, meaning a five-minute drive north puts you on winding canyon roads with sweeping basin-to-ocean views. That geographic compression defines daily life: Santa Monica Boulevard and Sunset Boulevard cut through the city as its commercial spines, lined with a concentration of restaurants, design showrooms, and nightlife venues that would be remarkable in a city ten times its size, and the flat-to-gently-sloping terrain between those corridors makes most errands genuinely walkable. The entertainment and hospitality industries anchor much of the local economy, and the broader Los Angeles job market surrounds the city on all sides, though commuting outward on surface streets or the 101 can be grinding. With a median home price above $969,000 against a median household income near $95,000, the price-to-income ratio exceeds 10:1 — squarely in rent-dominated territory, and median rent itself sits above $2,100. Climate softens the cost sting: annual daytime highs average 76°F with nearly ten hours of sunshine daily, and nighttime lows rarely dip below the mid-50s, making year-round outdoor dining and evening walks along the Sunset Strip a default rather than a luxury. Property crime runs notably high at roughly 6,000 per 100,000, driven heavily by larceny, a pattern common in commercial-heavy, high-foot-traffic districts. West Hollywood is essentially a dense urban village borrowing its mountain backdrop and job market from greater Los Angeles while paying a steep premium for the privilege of not needing a car for dinner.
